2:
Welcome everyone. (Introduce yourself briefly)
First I want to thank Elisabeth to let me talk about my hobbies here with you, but this talk is about how YOU can build your own amazing software with AI.
If any questions pop up during the talk just write them in the chat and we will look at them in the end.
3:
I've spent the last 6 months on projects like this. If you're thinking about building something of your own with AI, here are some good reasons for that.

For me personaly it was to take back the joy of developing. As you all know, AI releases get better and better. And the joy of developing can get lost not writing code anymore. A hobby project lets you build applications you could never have built before.

Other questions I wanted to answer.
• Can a real app or game be built with AI first?
• Will a larger project get more and more bugs. Does it stay scalable and stable, or get sloppy over time?
• How much supervision does it need?
• And how can we become a better prompt programmers?

My examples: 
- a chess engine
- a jetpack multiplayer 2D platform retro game
- a 3D first-person, sci-fi game, inspired by Descent, which I played a lot in the 90s.
4:
These are some of my findings I want to share. The rest of the talk shows where they come from.

- Split tasks into sub-tasks for better results.
- Guide the AI as much as possible, review and test.
- AI might be a better coder than you think.
5:
I started coding as a kid in the 80s.

Before going professional in 2001, I spent a few years as a math and chemistry teacher.

After I studied again, (system development) I got hired at OMX and later product companies, med tech and consulting. I came to SEB two and a half years ago and have been a developer in the HULT team since.

Programming has always been my hobby too. I've spent far too many hours improving my chess engines over the years.

I have two grown daughters, and I got married this spring.
6:
A good advice for a hobby project might be to pick a goal you can measure. Mine was to get ranked on CCRL. It is a site that rates computer chess engines. My goal was to reach 2000 Elo.

Elo is a rating where the gap between two players predicts the result. 200 points stronger means you win roughly 75% of the games played. A beginner is around 800, a strong club player around 2000, and grandmasters start at about 2500.

My first engine was in VB.net and never made a good move. I read up on the theory and the pseudocode and kept going. Second attempt, in C#: better moves, but too slow. Third attempt in plain C was about 40 times faster. That's called ChessMatrix. It has Elo 1863, around place 700 globally on CCRL. Close to my goal, but not quite there.

This summer I built ZeroG with Antigravity and Gemini 3.6 Flash. If you try this, my advice would be to break the work into small steps, the same ones you'd take if you wrote it yourself. Unit test, performance test and refactor everything. And gate every change. Dont commit without  a significant improvement. I let it play 400 games against the previous version.

The result was Elo 2666, place 398 on CCRL. That's over 800 Elo stronger than years of my own work.

Also expect it to handle hard bugs. At one point the engine started playing invalid moves. That kind of bug used to be a nightmare for me, because the search functions are long, complicated and recursive. Let the AI work at it: it debugged step by step for a long time and pinpointed the exact error.

This was one of the moments I realized AI is so much better at coding than me.
7:
Quick look under the hood. The first job of any engine is move generation which list every legal move.

The board is doing exactly that now. From the start position it makes and unmakes each of White's 20 moves. That's depth 1.

(Click Depth 2). For each of White's 20 moves, Black has 20 replies. 400 positions.

Click Depth 3: 8,902 positions. Point at the table: depth 6 is already 119 million. It grows roughly 30 times per move. Engines generate millions of positions per second, and it still isn't enough to look at everything.

That's why move generation has to be fast and exactly right. One wrong move in here and the whole search is wrong. If you build one, this is where unit tests save you, and where you can lean on the AI's step-by-step debugging.

The best engines needs to search atleast 25 to 30 moves ahead.
8:
Since you can't look at everything, the engine has to be smart about what it looks at.

• The engine picks the move best for it, and assume the opponent picks the move best for them. That's called the minimax algorithm.
• Pruning skips lines that can't change the answer. That's called alpha-beta pruning.
• At the leaf node the position is evaluated. That is at the end of each line. It considers material, piece placement, king safety, etc.

Note that this kind of 'AI' does a search, plus a scoring function. It is not a language model. The language model helps you write it.
9:
Alpha-beta is just the start. You need many more pruning techniques to make the search strong. Three examples:

• Null move pruning: let the opponent move twice in a row. If you're still clearly winning even after giving away a free move, the position is so good you don't need to search it fully.
• Late move reductions: sort moves so the most promising come first. Search moves late in the list less deeply. If one surprises you, search it again at full depth.
• Futility pruning: close to the end of the search, if you're far behind and a quiet move can't possibly make up the difference, skip it.
There are many more of these examples to make the search perform better.

Each one is a trade-off: search less, risk missing something. Only a big test like the 400 games tells you if it's worth it.

The evaluation is just as important. A deep search with a bad evaluation still picks bad moves. In the past evaluation was hand-written: material, piece placement, king safety, with weights tuned by hand.
Today, engines use a trained neural network for leaf node evaluation. It's trained on millions of positions and designed to update quickly as moves are made. That was one of the biggest jumps in engine strength in recent years.
10:
In a chess engine, performance is important. The faster the search, the deeper it sees, and the stronger it plays.

So ask the AI to set up benchmarking: small programs that run move generation, search and evaluate on fixed positions and measure the speed. On top of that, a profiler. I was using a Mac and the profiler tool was Valgrind's Callgrind. Make it all one command so it is easy to excecute repetedly.

Then let the AI read the profiler output itself. It's a long text report of call stacks and sample counts, which is tedious to read yourself. The AI quickly points out the hot spots, fixes them, re-runs the benchmark and confirms the speed-up.

Save the workflow as a skill, so the AI knows how to profile the project next time.

Give the AI a way to measure. With hard numbers it can find and fix problems on its own, and show that the fix worked.
11:
Aim for improvements you can measure.

A lot of talk about AI productivity is gut feeling: 'it feels faster', 'the code seems better'. That's hard to prove.

If your domain allows it, find a hard metric. In chess, Elo comes from games played. Every change to ZeroG had to pass the gate: 400 games against the previous version, with a significant improvement. If it didn't, it was rejected, no matter how good the code looked.

And use an independent judge where you can. CCRL rates engines independently, by playing them against other engines.

The comparison is fair: years of my own work by hand gave 1863 Elo. One summer with AI gave 2666. That's over 800 Elo improvement. And this is public data on CCRL website.

So when you can benchmark, do it.
12:
Next example: Jetpack. A good way to start is to make a simple game you like to play yourself. Mine was a retro 2D platformer where you fly a jetpack, collect emeralds, avoiding enemies and get to the next level.

I used Antigravity with Gemini 3.8, which had just been released. It was a big improvement over 3.6 Flash, both in performance and in speed. Development took less than a month.

You don't have to get the choice of language right from the start. Gemini chose JavaScript when I let it decide. Later I asked it to convert the whole thing to TypeScript, which it did without much trouble.

The hardest part for the AI was the turns in the maze, how the jetpack moves when you change direction in the air. It took several prompts and a lot of play testing before it felt natural and easy to steer.

You can generate all graphics and sound from prompts. Gemini made them in retro style as I requested.

If you need something similar to the music in jetpack you can prompt Gemini to take old classical melodies and play them in retro game style. I used for example Grieg's Hall of the Mountain King, Brahms' Hungarian Dance No. 5, Vivaldi, Mozart, Bach's Toccata and Fugue. (Click the screenshots: the music playing is from stage 6.)

And share your game. I deployed it and also played it online with friends and family, including multiplayer. It's now free for everyone to play and has been played by about 60 players so far. The source is also open on GitHub.
13:
Some lessons I want to share from development of Jetpack.

When the AI struggles with a bug for a while, code quality easily gets worse. It tries one fix after another, and the leftovers stay in the code. So once the bug is fixed, prompt the AI to clean up the code.

For the AI to work well, keep the code in good shape: a good architecture, types and variables properly named, files and functions that aren't too large, not much duplicated code, and so on.

Use AI for refactoring. It's fast, it makes good changes. New bugs were never intruduced when it did refactoring.

Set up code coverage. Let the AI do that. I asked Gemini, and it did all of it itself. It chose c8, which is a coverage tool in Node. It wrapped the whole test suite (about 40 test scripts) in one command, and configured it to create a report for the game client and the server, as plain text, and an HTML report.
Then prompt AI to use it as input. The text report is a table of every file and which lines are never run. Let the AI read the report, pick the gaps and write new unit tests for them. Very quickly it added tests for the game, the multiplayer controller and the networking code.
About 65% of jetpacks functions are covered. That's a lot for a hobby game, and it took very little effort.
This is similar to what I did with the profiler. When the AI can measure, it finds the gaps on its own.
14:
Now the main example: Terminal Depth.

A tip: Before you start your dream project test to do a smaller project first. Jetpack was really just a first test, to see whether it was worth starting on my dream project: a modern version of a game I played a lot in the 90s. A 3D first-person shooter with six degrees of freedom, flying in tunnels and mines.

Don't be afraid of new ground. This was a much bigger step than Jetpack: 3D modelling and integrating with a real game engine. I looked at Unreal but selected Godot.

(Click the video to play some gameplay.)
15:
Here's a pipeline you can use. Unlike with Jetpack, you use a different AI tool for each job.

First, use ChatGPT to create concept images: enemies, the player's spaceship, weapons and other items in the game.

Then use that image to generate a 3D model with Meshy.ai, an AI tool made specifically for that purpose.

Copy the 3D models into the game's source code, and ask your coding AI to import them into the game. I used Gemini, and later Claude.

Now and then, use Blender for small manual adjustments to the AI-generated models, or to reduce the number of polygons for performance reasons.
16:
For music, try Google Gemini's online chat, which has a music plugin.

For sound effects, try ElevenLabs (elevenlabs.io).

For the game engine I chose Godot, with C# for the game logic.

That's the big difference from Jetpack, where one AI did almost everything. Here several AI tools each do one job, and the coding-AI puts it all into the game.
17:
To give you an idea of what you can build: some facts about Terminal Depth.

The first commit was on the 11th of September, about two and a half months ago.

On the left, the code: well over a hundred thousand lines. Most of it is C# game code, but there is almost as much test code as game code, plus a whole pipeline of Python and GDScript tooling for 3D models, textures, headless checks and rendering.

On the right, the content: close to a hundred scenes, dozens of sound effects, 3D models and textures, story voice lines, different enemy types, rooms and corridors, music, and several playable levels.

All in all, the downloadable game is around 600 MB.

In two months, I estimated that I only spent 150 hours on this hobby project. It is not quite finished but almost.
18:
How do you keep a big project like this on track with AI? With rules and skills.

Keep the project instructions in a AGENTS.md file, so Gemini and Claude read the same rules. CLAUDE.md can just import it.

Ask the AI after every prompt propse rules that you review before adding them to the project. Dont forget to sometime prompt ai to organize its rules.
It put 12 detailed rules in small files: audio, lighting, save/load, testing, coding standards and so on. Let each rule say which file paths it applies to, so it only loads when the AI works in that area. That keeps the context smaller.

Skills are step-by-step procedures the AI finds by their description. And let the AI build them, for example the 3D model pipeline, model performance optimization, and level assembly.

Add a few hard rules of your own like: 
 - never commit, so you review briefly and commit yourself.
 - Zero-warning build, so that every warning fails the build.

And after every propmpt, have the AI reflect on what was hard and propose improvements to the rules or skills, so you can approve those suggestions with a simple yes. These rules grew with the project.

Have the AI point at Technical debt, not fix it on its own. Otherwise every small task turns into a big refactor. Collect it and run dedicated cleanup passes, with saved prompts and written plans.
19:
Let me sum up the advice in one slide.

Start small. Jetpack was my test run before Terminal Depth. Learn how the tools work on something you can finish, THEN go for the dream project.

Set a measurable goal, like the CCRL ranking for the chess engine. Where every change had to prove itself: if it doesn't measurably help, throw it away.

Split the work into small steps, the same steps you'd take if you wrote the code yourself. Big vague prompts give big vague results.

Give the AI ways to measure its own work: tests, coverage, benchmarks and a profiler. Then it can check itself instead of guessing.

Keep the code clean. After a long bug hunt, clean up the leftovers, and sometimes prompt to refactor. Messy code makes the AI worse too.

And write the rules and skills together with the AI. Let it propose them; YOU review and commit.
20:
A disclaimer before we wrap up. None of these methods produce bug-free code. Tests, gates and benchmarks catch a lot, but not everything.

In a hobby project, developing speed is the fun part. When we build a banking app, I don't think we should have that speed.

So for banking apps everything you commit, you need to read the code and understand it. The AI writes it, but you own it.

Don't code too fast.
